passages.t: ‘I love the LORD, for He has heard my voice’
passages.happening:
This psalm begins with a simple confession. “I love the LORD, for He has heard my voice” (verse 1). Because God has bent down to listen, “I will call on Him as long as I live” (verse 2).

Then the singer tells what happened. “The ropes of death entangled me; the anguish of Sheol overcame me; I was confronted by trouble and sorrow” (verse 3). He cried out, “O LORD, deliver my soul!” (verse 4). And God did.

“The LORD is gracious and righteous; our God is full of compassion” (verse 5). “I was helpless, and He saved me” (verse 6). So he speaks to himself: “Return to your rest, O my soul, for the LORD has been good to you” (verse 7). God has saved his life, his eyes from tears, and his feet from stumbling (verse 8). “I will walk before the LORD in the land of the living” (verse 9).

He remembers how he felt when things were worst. “I believed, therefore I said, ‘I am greatly afflicted’” (verse 10). In his panic he said, “All men are liars!” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
This is a song of thanks for a rescue from death, perhaps from a deadly illness. The psalm does not say what the danger was. It borrows older words. ‘The ropes of death’ echo David's song: “The cords of death encompassed me” (Psalm 18:4). Verse 8 echoes Psalm 56:13. Sheol, the place of the dead, is explained on the book page.

‘Return to your rest, O my soul’ is a person talking to himself, telling his frightened heart that it can settle down now. The psalms often do this (compare Psalm 42 and 43, ‘Why are you downcast, O my soul?’).

Verses 10 and 11 are hard Hebrew, and translations differ. The BSB's reading is that he kept believing even while he said how bad things were, and that in his alarm he decided no human help could be trusted.

This psalm is part of the Hallel, sung at Passover, as the note on Psalm 113 explains.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 10 in the form of the Greek Old Testament: “I believed, therefore I have spoken” (2 Corinthians 4:13). He uses it to say that believers who suffer still speak of their faith.

Paul also echoes verse 11: “Let God be true and every man a liar” (Romans 3:4).
passages.asks:
Verse 2 is worth stopping on. Because God has listened, the singer will keep praying for the rest of his life. Answered prayer is not the end of prayer. It is a reason for more.

And verse 7 gives words for a restless mind. When you have been through a hard time and your heart is still racing, you may say to yourself what this man said: ‘Return to your rest, O my soul.’

passages.t: ‘How can I repay the LORD?’ and ‘Precious in the sight of the LORD’
passages.happening:
Now the singer asks a question. “How can I repay the LORD for all His goodness to me?” (verse 12). He answers it himself. “I will lift the cup of salvation and call on the name of the LORD” (verse 13). “I will fulfill my vows to the LORD in the presence of all His people” (verse 14).

Then comes a line many grieving people have held on to. “Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of His saints” (verse 15).

He calls himself God's servant twice over, “the son of Your maidservant” (verse 16). And yet, “You have broken my bonds” (verse 16). He will bring a sacrifice of thanks and keep his promises in the temple courts, in Jerusalem (verses 17 to 19). The psalm ends, “Hallelujah!” (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
In danger, an Israelite often made a vow: a promise to bring an offering to God if he was rescued. Once he was safe, he went to the temple to keep it, in front of everyone. The ‘sacrifice of thanksgiving’ (verse 17) was shared in a meal with family and friends, and the rescued person told his story (Leviticus 7:12 describes the offering).

‘The cup of salvation’ (verse 13) was probably a cup of wine poured out or drunk at that meal, to give thanks for being saved.

‘Precious’ in verse 15 translates a Hebrew word used for rare jewels. It means costly and weighty. The verse does not mean that God is glad when his faithful people die. It means their death is costly to him. He does not let it happen lightly or forget it.

‘The son of Your maidservant’ was a slave born in a household, who belonged to it from birth (Exodus 21:4 shows the custom). The singer says he belongs to God completely. And this master has not tied him down. He has set him free.
passages.later:
At the Last Supper, Jesus took a cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (1 Corinthians 11:25). In Gethsemane he spoke of a different cup: “My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from Me” (Matthew 26:39).

Paul echoes the free servant of verse 16: “now that you have been set free from sin and have become slaves to God, the fruit you reap leads to holiness” (Romans 6:22). Hebrews calls believers to “continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (Hebrews 13:15).
passages.hard:
A word for anyone who is grieving. Verse 15 can be a comfort to anyone who has lost someone who loved God. It says that the death of someone who belonged to God mattered to God. It was not small or unseen. It does not say that their death was good, or that you should not grieve. Jesus wept at his friend's grave (John 11:35). Paul wrote to grieving believers so “that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). He did not tell them not to grieve.

If your grief is heavy, please do not carry it alone. Tell someone you trust: a pastor, a friend, a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks:
What can you give God for all his goodness? The psalm's answer is surprising. You cannot repay him. You can only take more from him (lift the cup of salvation), call on him again, and keep your promises in front of others.

Thanks, in Psalm 116, is not private. It is told to God's people. Is there a rescue in your life that you have never thanked God for out loud?
